content.thinking:
I'm putting the postmortem together from the key facts: p95 latency went up from its baseline during the broken window, with no rise in errors and no customer loss. The change P2 deployed revision 5e07d73 at 03:50:19, and the rollback at T20 was confirmed at T23. I'm also questioning whether the "account pages loaded slowly" symptom actually ties the latency to account pages.

I'm weighing whether to call the symptom "account pages" or something broader, since the latency series is service-wide. I'm settling on the shop and noting that the slowest requests to io-shop took far longer, with no rise in failures. Next I'm connecting the onset to revision 5e07d73, which was running on every replica from the 03:50:19 deploy.

I'm checking whether the earlier deploy, P1, could explain the slowdown. The metrics read covers the 360 minutes leading up to the onset, and it shows the service healthy in that window, so I'm ruling P1 out. The rollback to that earlier revision, confirmed at T23, also left the service recovering, which backs that up. I'm also ruling out feature flag changes, since the flag history shows none.

I'm settling the causal chain now: revision 5e07d73 went out on every replica with the 03:50:19 deploy, which lines up with the onset. I'm also checking the slower average_spend_per_item code, where a loop re-sums all earlier purchases for each one, so the work grows with the square of a shopper's purchase count. Whether that loop actually explains the latency still depends on a reading I haven't confirmed by running it.

I'm checking whether the loop in average_spend_per_item really accounts for the slowdown, and I'm treating the diff as the only source change, which the rollback supports. The render path calls that function whenever neither flag is set, and no flag changes came back, so the chain holds at this step.

I'm laying out the contributing factors now, starting with the missing check on how average_spend_per_item scales for shoppers with long purchase histories, since the existing tests only cover small accounts.

I'm turning to the contributing factors next. The missing performance check on long purchase histories is already set down, and I'm considering a second factor: no one was paged, even though the alert fired. That doesn't look like something that shortened the outage, so I'm treating it as a gap in how things went rather than a contributing cause, and proposing an item that routes this alert to on-call.

I'm working out the contributing factors now: the performance check on long purchase histories was never run before the change shipped, and the deploy went to all three replicas with no staged rollout or canary check I could see. I'm also drafting action items, starting with a test to

I'm drafting the action items now, starting with a performance check in io-shop's CI that runs the account-page summary functions against accounts with long purchase histories and fails any change whose cost grows past a set bound. For the canary gap, I'm proposing that io-shop deploys go to one replica first and hold while its p95 latency is compared against the replicas still on the earlier revision. I'm also adding a process item to route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to on-call paging, and I'm skipping the code-review checklist idea.

Now I'm listing what went well: the onset was placed at the deploy, all replicas were confirmed on the same revision, the rollback took effect, and a draft fix was proposed.

I'm noting that the change left nothing alerting a person, so there was no on-call incident tied to it. I'm also checking that the quadratic loop is still in revision 5e07d73, which means it would return if automatic sync got turned on before the fix merged or the service was redeployed.

I'm settling the wording of the root-cause line: the slow calculation is still in revision 5e07d73, so redeploying it would slow the account pages again. I'm listing the assumptions behind the chain, including that the service-wide latency series reflects what shoppers saw on account pages, that the lifetime-average path runs when no flags are set, and that shoppers have long purchase histories, which I haven't measured.

I'm finishing the root-cause line: revision 5e07d73 rewrote the average-spend calculation so it repeats the same summing for every past purchase, so the more a shopper has bought, the more work each page load does. The rollback confirming the revision backs this up, and the diff shows that this is the only source change.

I'm checking how the lifetime figure is calculated, since average_spend_per_item re-sums the prices of every earlier purchase for each one and keeps only the final pass, so the work per call grows faster as a shopper's history gets longer. The account page takes that path whenever neither rollout flag is set, and I'm noting that I haven't run this yet, so it stays a reading for now. Next I'm tracing whether shopper requests to io-shop match that pattern.

I'm laying out the chain step by step: the latency rose during the window, with no rise in errors, and the revision went out on the deploy at the same minute the onset is placed, with every replica on it. I'm checking the flag history as ruled out for the change.

I'm writing up the root-cause line now: the revision rewrote average_spend_per_item so that each account page's lifetime figure does work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count, which slows the responses.

action_items.item: Add a check to io-shop's pipeline that times the account-page summary functions on accounts with long purchase histories and fails any change whose cost grows beyond a set bound.
Roll io-shop deployments out to a canary replica first, and hold the rollout while that replica's p95 latency is compared with replicas still on the earlier revision.
Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' requests to io-shop were answered far more slowly than usual, while no larger share of them failed than before.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy P1 of revision 70dbcfde2b549d110a3817d92d60b6dd9786e78b: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset, and rolling back to it returned the service to normal, which was confirmed.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider's history showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus.

causal_chain.step: Deploy P2 by kuki at {P2.1} put revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 on io-shop, in the minute the onset was placed in. As of {T11.1}, all replicas ran that revision, so the slowdown was not a split between versions.

The revision rewrote average_spend_per_item, the function render_spend_summary calls for the account page's lifetime figure when neither rollout flag is set. It replaced dividing the account's carried total by its number of purchases with a loop that, for each purchase, re-sums the prices of every purchase up to that one.
Each call now did work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count instead of a single division, so pages that showed the figure took far longer to compute.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A software update changed how the shop works out a shopper's average spend per item: it now adds up the shopper's past purchases again for each purchase in turn, so the more a shopper had bought, the more work each page took.

contributing_factors.factor: No check of how long the account-page calculations take on a long purchase history was seen before the change went out. The tests at the revision check only correct values, on accounts with a handful of purchases.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A check timing average_spend_per_item on a long history would have failed on the prefix-re-summing loop, and the revision would have been stopped before it reached production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No staged or canary rollout was seen: the revision reached every replica, with nothing seen comparing latency on new replicas against the earlier revision before the rollout completed.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The slowdown would have reached only part of the traffic and could have halted the rollout before every shopper's requests were slowed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read that every replica ran revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655, which tied the slowdown to that deploy and ruled out a split between versions.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else, which ruled out a flag as the trigger.
The Mitigation Agent rolled back the deployment of io-shop for C1.
The Mitigation Agent confirmed the rollback once the service was no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #553 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert fired but was not linked to an on-call incident, so no person was called in to the response.

input.root_cause: Revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 rewrote average_spend_per_item so that, for every purchase in an account's history, it re-sums the prices of all purchases up to that point and keeps only the last pass. The work per call therefore grows with the square of the number of purchases, where before it was a single division of the account's carried total. render_spend_summary takes this path for the account page's figure whenever neither rollout flag is set.
input.still_at_risk: Revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 still holds the slow calculation, and deploying it or anything built on it again would slow the shop's responses in the same way.
input.symptom: Shoppers' requests to the shop were answered far more slowly than usual
